title: Why doubling up fails
objectives: Show why a doubling strategy cannot beat a fair game.

screens.title: Double after a loss
screens.prose: You hold £7 and bet £1 on a fair coin. After a loss you double the stake; after a win you stop. £7 funds stakes of £1, £2 and £4.

state.caption: One cycle: three doublings at most.

screens.question: What is your expected gain from one cycle, in pounds?

hints.text: A win at any stage leaves you £1 up.
You lose all £7 only if all three bets lose: chance $\tfrac18$.

feedback.correct: Zero: the cycle is a fair bet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each outcome by its chance.

byKey.one: You counted only the wins. One cycle in eight loses £7.
byKey.p: That is the chance of winning £1, not the expected gain.

explain.text: You win £1 with chance $\tfrac78$ and lose £7 with chance $\tfrac18$. The expected gain is $\tfrac78 - \tfrac78 = 0$. The strategy reshapes the risk but cannot add value.

screens.title: Many cycles
screens.prose: Now a doubler starts with £63 and plays cycle after cycle on a fair coin. The top panel is the coin; the bottom panel is the bankroll. Press New paths a few times.

state.caption: Doubling from £1 with £63. The lower panel is the bankroll.

screens.question: What does the bankroll path look like?

options.text: Small steady gains, then a rare sharp drop
A steady climb that never falls
options.why: Watch longer: a run of losses takes the whole doubled stake at once.

options.text: Large swings up and down, evenly balanced
options.why: The gains are small and frequent; the losses are rare and large. The shape is lopsided.

hints.text: Most steps add £1 over a cycle.
A run of six losses costs £63 in one go.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the bottom panel over several runs.

explain.text: Each cycle usually adds £1, so the bankroll creeps up. A run of losses then removes many cycles' gains at once. On average the two cancel.

screens.title: Ten doublings
screens.prose: Now start with £1,023 and double from £1 after each loss. The ledger shows what each bet costs.

columns: Lost so far if it loses

state.caption: Double after each loss; stop at the first win. £1,023 funds ten bets.

screens.question: Fill in the chance of losing the cycle and the expected gain. Give the chance as a fraction or to six decimal places.

hints.text: The cycle fails only if all ten bets lose.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Ten fair losses in a row have chance $(\tfrac12)^{10} = \tfrac{1}{1024}$.
byKey.r1c1: Weight the £1 win by $\tfrac{1023}{1024}$ and the £1,023 loss by $\tfrac{1}{1024}$.

explain.text: The cycle loses with chance $\tfrac{1}{1024} \approx 0.000977$. Then it costs £1,023, which exactly cancels the £1 won the rest of the time. The loss is sized to match its rarity.

screens.title: On a real wheel
screens.prose: The same ten doublings, betting on red at a European wheel. Red wins with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$ and pays evens.

columns: Lost so far if it loses

state.caption: Double after each loss; stop at the first win. £1,023 funds ten bets.

screens.question: What is the expected gain per cycle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The cycle loses with chance $q^{10}$, where $q = \tfrac{19}{37}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $q = \tfrac{19}{37}$ for a loss.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer. Each red bet loses slightly more often than it wins.
byKey.one: That is the edge on one £1 bet. A cycle stakes up to £1,023.
byKey.pos: Check the sign. The rare loss outweighs the wins.

explain.text: $q^{10} = (\tfrac{19}{37})^{10} \approx 0.001275$, so the gain is $1 - 1024 \times 0.001275 \approx -0.3056$. A simulation of 400,000 cycles agrees within its noise. Doubling turns a small edge against you into a larger loss per cycle.

screens.title: Too rare to matter?
screens.prose: A friend plays the £1,023 doubling on a fair coin. He says ten losses in a row are so rare that the strategy is safe money.
screens.question: What is wrong with his reasoning?

options.text: The rare loss is sized to cancel the steady wins, so the expectation stays 0
Nothing: a chance of $\tfrac{1}{1024}$ can be ignored
options.why: Its size is £1,023, a thousand cycles of winnings. Rare and large still counts.

options.text: After nine losses, a tenth is less likely
options.why: That is the gambler's fallacy. The tenth flip is still fair.

options.text: Losses get likelier as the stakes grow
options.why: Every bet is a fair coin, whatever the stake.

hints.text: Multiply the chance by the size.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the loss by its size, not only its chance.

byKey.b: You looked only at the chance. The loss is £1,023, so it carries as much weight as all the wins.
byKey.c: That is the gambler's fallacy from conditional l22. Each flip is fair.

explain.text: The loss has chance $\tfrac{1}{1024}$ and size £1,023, exactly cancelling the steady £1 wins. Over 1,000 cycles the chance of at least one disaster is about 62%. Rare does not mean small.

screens.title: Optional stopping
screens.prose:
Every doubler met the same wall. **Optional stopping**: in a fair game with a finite bankroll, no rule for when to stop can raise the expected gain. A rule that must end within a fixed number of bets leaves it exactly unchanged:

$$E[X_\tau] = X_0.$$

A doubling cycle ends within $n$ bets, so it qualifies. In an unfair game, every rule keeps the expected loss.
screens.question: A gambler bets £1 on a fair coin and stops when £5 ahead or after 100 bets. What is the expected gain?

options.why: He reaches £5 up only some of the time; the other runs end below.
Stopping when ahead feels like an edge, but the runs that end behind cancel it.

hints.text: Is the game fair, and is the time bounded?
Both: fair bets and at most 100 of them.
So the expected gain stays at £0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply optional stopping.

explain.text: The game is fair and stops within 100 bets, so the expected gain is £0. With unlimited money and time the doubler wins £1 for sure, but the expected stake he must risk is infinite. No real bankroll can fund that.

screens.title: Why it is zero
screens.prose: Show that any doubling cycle on a fair coin has expected gain 0. It starts at £1 and allows $n$ bets.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: A win at any of the $n$ bets leaves you £1 up: each stake covers the earlier losses plus £1.
The cycle fails only if all $n$ bets lose, with chance $2^{-n}$.
The chance of failing tends to 0 as $n$ grows, so the gain tends to £1.
lines.why: The loss grows as fast as its chance shrinks. Their product is $1 - 2^{-n}$, exactly the chance of winning £1.

hints.text: Find the win, the failure chance and the failure size.
The failure chance and size can go in either order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from what a win gives.

byKey.d1: The failure chance halves and the loss about doubles, so their product is $1 - 2^{-n}$, not 1. That is exactly the chance of the £1 win, so the two cancel.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the limit argument belongs.

explain.text: The failure chance halves with each extra bet, and the failure cost doubles. So their product, $2^{-n}(2^n - 1)$, cancels the win. No $n$ escapes it.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each; keep your own time and say each argument aloud. Give four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Chance of seven losses in a row on a fair coin?
A doubling cycle with £63 on a fair coin. Expected gain (£)?
The same £63 cycle on European red. Expected gain (£)?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: A fair cycle has expected gain 0 whatever the bankroll.

explain.text: Seven losses have chance $\tfrac{1}{128} \approx 0.0078$. A fair cycle is worth £0 for any bankroll. On red the £63 cycle loses about £0.17, since $1 - 64 \times 0.01834 \approx -0.1735$.

screens.title: Drill: the same shape
screens.prose: One more, about a minute. A fund sells options that rarely pay out. Most months it keeps a small premium; now and then it pays a large sum.
screens.question: Which strategy has the same shape of profit and loss?

options.why: That is the mirror image: small steady losses and rare large gains.
Kelly sizing keeps losses in proportion to wealth. It has no hidden cliff.

options.text: Hedging a bet at fair odds
options.why: A fair hedge removes variance. It does not create a rare large loss.

hints.text: Describe the profit and loss in words.
Small, frequent gains; rare, large losses.
Which strategy in this lesson looked like that?

feedback.correct: Doubling: small steady gains and a rare large loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match small steady gains with a rare large loss.

byKey.b: You flipped the shape. Lottery tickets lose a little often and win big rarely.

explain.text: Selling options that rarely pay out collects small premiums and sometimes pays a large sum. That is the doubler's bankroll: a steady climb and a cliff. A good track record says little about the cliff.

screens.title: Follow-up: a smaller bankroll
screens.prose: You found $-0.3056$ for ten doublings on European red. The interviewer asks about £127, enough for seven doublings.
screens.question: What is the expected gain per cycle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: £127 funds stakes of £1 to £64: seven bets.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use seven bets and $q = \tfrac{19}{37}$.

byKey.ten: That is the ten-doubling answer. Seven doublings risk less per cycle.
byKey.pos: Check the sign. The rare loss outweighs the wins.

explain.text: $q^7 \approx 0.009416$, so the gain is $1 - 128 \times 0.009416 \approx -0.2052$. A simulation of 400,000 cycles agrees within its noise. Smaller bankrolls lose less per cycle but fail more often.

screens.title: Selling volatility
screens.prose: A fund sells options each month. With chance 0.98 it keeps a £1,000 premium. With chance 0.02 the options pay out and the fund loses $L$.
screens.question: For what loss $L$, in pounds, is the expected monthly profit zero?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equate the expected premium with the expected loss.

byKey.fifty: You used $1000/0.02$. The premium comes only in the good months, with chance 0.98.
byKey.prem: That is the premium. The loss must be far larger to balance it.

explain.text: $0.98 \times 1000 = 980$, so $L = 980/0.02 = £49{,}000$. Thirty good months in a row have chance $0.98^{30} \approx 0.55$, so a clean record proves little. It is a doubling scheme in disguise.

ideas: Doubling wins a small amount often and loses a large amount rarely; on a fair coin they cancel exactly.
Optional stopping: with a finite bankroll, no stopping rule can raise a fair game's expectation, and one that must end within a fixed number of bets leaves it unchanged.
On an unfair game doubling enlarges the loss per cycle. Selling rarely paying options has the same shape.
summary.trap: Calling the strategy safe because ten losses in a row are rare. The loss is sized to cancel the wins.

quiz.prose: A doubler has unlimited money and unlimited time, on a fair coin.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: He wins £1 for sure, but the expected stake he must risk is infinite
He has found a sure profit that works in practice
options.why: It needs unlimited money. With any real bankroll the expected gain is 0.

options.text: His expected gain is still negative
options.why: On a fair coin each bet is fair. The trouble is the size of the risk, not a negative mean.

feedback.correct: A sure £1, at an infinite expected risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the guarantee needs.

explain.text: With no limit, a head eventually comes and he is £1 up. The money he must risk before then has infinite expectation. This edge case is why optional stopping needs a finite bankroll.

quiz.prose: A doubler holds £15 and plays one cycle on a fair coin.
quiz.question: What is the chance the cycle fails? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the bets £15 funds.

byKey.eighth: That is three bets. £15 funds four: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8.
byKey.fifteen: You took $\tfrac{1}{15}$. Count bets, not pounds.

explain.text: £15 funds stakes of £1, £2, £4 and £8: four bets. All four lose with chance $\tfrac{1}{16}$.

quiz.prose: A doubler with £1,023 plays 1,000 cycles on a fair coin, topping up after any loss.
quiz.question: What is the chance of at least one failed cycle? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all 1,000 cycles succeed.

byKey.tiny: That is the chance for one cycle. Over 1,000 cycles it adds up.
byKey.approx: You multiplied $\tfrac{1}{1024}$ by 1,000. Use the chance that none fail instead.

explain.text: Every cycle succeeds with chance $\tfrac{1023}{1024}$, so all 1,000 succeed with $(\tfrac{1023}{1024})^{1000} \approx 0.376$. At least one fails with about 0.6236. The rare event becomes likely over a long career.
